newsitem.title: USA: Customers set to fund $1 bln U.S. payphone rebates.
newsitem.headline: Customers set to fund $1 bln U.S. payphone rebates.

text.p: So you think all your toll free calls are free? Think again.

The long distance industry has just begun raising from customers almost $1 billion a year it has been ordered to pay to payphone firms to compensate them for revenue lost because of toll free numbers and calling cards used at payphones.

AT&T Corp on Tuesday notified in advertisements that it would increase 1-800 number rates by three percent and add a $0.15 surcharge on business calling cards to pay rebates ordered by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).
It is not just business customers who pay.
Sprint Corp said a consumer long distance tariff rate increase it filed on some calling plans in December was partly to pay for this compensation.
"It is a major issue in the industry," said Mike Lordi, an AT&T spokesman. "Opposition was strong right from the start," he added.

The 1996 Telecom Act included clauses to allow payphone operators, which are mostly regional Bells but also include a number of independent telephone companies, to be compensated for non-cash calls made from their payphones.
The FCC was responsible for implementing this principle and in September announced a three stage process which would begin in November.

The first stage is a $45.85 per payphone monthly payment to owners of 350,000 private payphones, funded by the largest 21 long distance carriers which has just begun and will continue until October this year.
"Reluctantly, some of the payphone increases will be passed on," said a spokesman for Sprint, adding that the company was studying how to do this.

In April the 1.8 million public payphones owned by local telephone companies will also be covered by the monthly payment, bringing the annual total payment by the long distance industry to $986 million.
By October new billing systems are supposed to be ready that will allow long distance companies to track when payphones are used for toll-free and calling card calls.
This will allow the FCC's third phase, of a $0.35 per call surcharge on calling card and toll-free calls.
AT&T, MCI Communications Corp Sprint Corp and other carriers have jointly filed legal challenges to the FCC decision over the size of the surcharge, but the case is not expected to begin until May.

The regional Bells contend that the payments are if anything too low, and say that the billions the long distance industry makes from toll-free and calling card calls has been partly at their expense.
"We think 35 cents is more than fair to the long distance industry; if anything it is a little on the low side," said a spokesman for NYNEX Corp. ((-- New York Newsrom 212 859 1610))
